intent: Let the owner give an approved commit a release name.

edit.summary:
I changed `authoring/authoring.domain.yaml` so the owner can give an approved commit a release name. I didn't run any checks or scenarios.

- **Commit property:** `Commit` has a new optional `release_name` (string).
- **New action:** `name_release` is owner-only and requires a person. It sets `release_name` on the commit. It is modeled on `name_deputy`, and its status is `proposed`.
- **Approval rule:** A precondition, `approved`, denies the action unless the commit is already approved.
- **Transitions:** `name_release` is added to the `Commit` transition matrix as `recorded → recorded`, also `proposed`.

I didn't touch the delivery domain or the composition. I left the authoring `version` at 18, so bump it if your process expects that. There is no scenario for the new action. The action doesn't stop the owner from renaming a commit that already has a release name, because the request didn't say.

findings.problem: name_release writes to a commit that is already approved. Elsewhere an approved commit is treated as settled: check_commit, cite_evidence and name_deputy are all denied once target.approved is true, with reasons like 'An approved commit is settled'. The Commit object and the 'commit' glossary entry also say a commit is immutable and 'nothing is edited in place'. Nothing says that release_name is an allowed exception, and the new action's reason text does not mention it.
findings.where: authoring.domain.yaml, actions.name_release (precondition 'approved') versus cite_evidence/name_deputy 'not-approved' and glossary 'commit'

findings.problem: A release name can be overwritten any number of times, because name_release has no check that release_name is not already set. The same name can also go on several commits, because nothing enforces uniqueness. The stated purpose is that people can say 'the release' instead of a commit id, and that breaks if one name points to several commits or its target changes.
findings.where: authoring.domain.yaml, actions.name_release preconditions and effects; Commit.release_name

findings.problem: The change adds a Commit property and a new owner action to Authoring, but the domain version stays at 18. The composition pins authoring at interface 1, and the interface version is not raised for the new action and property. Consumers and the change check may therefore not see the interface change.

The release name is never used after it is set. The deliver action and the deliver_approved_commit handoff still send only the commit id to Delivery, and no glossary entry defines 'release'. Delivery's requests, scenarios and probes therefore still show only commit ids. The stated goal, 'people talk about releases', is not met where deployments are tracked.

name_release has no guard against a name already being set, and nothing makes release names unique. The owner can overwrite a commit's release name silently, or give the same name to two approved commits. When a newer approved commit supersedes an older one, both can end up with the same release name. That defeats the stated purpose of talking about a release instead of a commit id, because the name no longer identifies one commit. An empty string is also accepted as a name.

The glossary says a commit is an immutable snapshot and 'nothing is edited in place'. name_release now changes a field on an already approved commit after approval. name_deputy, cite_evidence and check_commit all say an approved commit is 'settled' and refuse changes, so name_release contradicts that stance. The glossary 'commit' and 'approval' entries were not updated to say a release name may be added after approval.
findings.where: authoring.domain.yaml, glossary.commit / actions.name_release vs. not-approved preconditions

findings.problem: The release name stops at the Commit. The deliver handoff and Delivery's DeliveryRequest carry only the commit id, so Delivery's requests, deployments and refusals still can't be referred to by release name. The stated goal is not met where releases are delivered and verified.

The new action has no scenario. Neither the approved-only precondition (a name on unapproved C3 should be denied) nor the owner-only restriction is exercised. The world has an approved commit C1 and unapproved C2 and C3, so the fixtures could support one. The declaration changed with no version bump (authoring is still version 18, with the interface unchanged) even though a new action was added to the interface.

name_release writes release_name onto a commit that is already approved. That conflicts with the glossary, which says a commit is immutable and 'nothing is edited in place'. It also conflicts with the settled-after-approval rules: cite_evidence and name_deputy are denied on an approved commit with the reason 'An approved commit is settled', and check_commit and record_check are denied likewise. name_release is the only action that edits an approved commit, and the change does not update the glossary or explain the exception.
findings.where: authoring.domain.yaml, action name_release (precondition 'approved'), glossary 'commit', actions name_deputy / cite_evidence not-approved

findings.problem: Nothing stops name_release from being run again on a commit that already has a release_name. The name can be silently overwritten, and an empty string is accepted. Nothing makes a release name unique, so two commits can share one and 'the release' becomes ambiguous. This defeats the stated purpose of giving people a stable name instead of a commit id.

The new action has no scenario and no fixture coverage. It is not tested that an unapproved commit such as C2 or C3 is denied by 'approved', that an approved commit such as C1 gets the name, or that the owner-only restriction holds. Delivery and the deliver_approved_commit handoff still identify releases only by commit id, so the release name does not reach delivery.

name_release has no check that the commit is not already named, and nothing makes a release name unique. The owner can silently rename a release, and two commits can carry the same name. People then cannot use the name in place of the commit id, which is the stated purpose of the change.

name_release is the first action that changes an approved commit. The other actions on Commit treat approval as final: check_commit, record_check, cite_evidence and name_deputy all say an approved commit is settled and is denied further changes. The glossary says a commit is immutable and nothing is edited in place. Naming a release after approval is not reconciled with those statements and may be inconsistent with them.
findings.where: authoring/authoring.domain.yaml, name_release 'approved' precondition vs. name_deputy/cite_evidence 'not-approved' preconditions and the glossary entry 'commit'

findings.problem: The release name is stored only on the Authoring Commit. The deliver_approved_commit handoff does not pass it to Delivery, and DeliveryRequest has no field for it. Delivery requests, probes and verification still show only the commit id, so the people who talk about releases do not see the name there.

The change adds an action, a property and a transition cell, but the domain version (18) and the interface version used in the composition (1) are unchanged. The new action is not covered by any scenario or world fixture. An approved commit such as C1 exists, but nothing exercises the 'approved' precondition or the owner-only actor.

name_release changes an approved commit after approval. The commit object is described as 'An immutable snapshot' and the glossary says 'Every change is a new commit; nothing is edited in place.' Other actions that touch a commit after approval are blocked: check_commit, cite_evidence and name_deputy all refuse with 'An approved commit is settled'. name_release does the reverse and only works on an approved commit. The rule that an approved commit is settled is not updated to allow this exception.
findings.where: authoring.domain.yaml, action name_release (precondition 'approved') versus glossary 'commit' and the not-approved preconditions on check_commit, cite_evidence and name_deputy

findings.problem: A release name can be set again at any time, because there is no precondition that the commit is not already named. Nothing makes names unique across commits, either. A release name could therefore be moved to another commit or reused, so it would not reliably identify one release, which is the reason for the change.

The release name stays on the Authoring commit and never reaches Delivery. The deliver_approved_commit handoff and the DeliveryRequest object carry only the commit id. The people who talk about deployments and verification will still see commit ids, so the stated purpose is not met where releases are delivered.

The domain gains a new action and a new Commit property, but the version stays at 18. The change adds no scenario that exercises name_release, such as owner-only, approved-only, or a denial on an unapproved commit such as C3, even though world fixtures for approved and unapproved commits exist.
